summary:
Coahuila de Zaragoza, one of Mexico's states, runs its own administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The congress of Coahuila passed the Ley del Registro Civil del Estado de Coahuila in 2018; articles 124 to 128 of that law establish the administrative procedure by which a person's self-identified gender identity is recognised. Human Rights Watch's March 2025 tracker of legal gender recognition across Mexico's states records Coahuila among those that have legislated such a procedure and links the official gazette text of the reform at articles 124 to 128.

The law defines the concept it administers. Article 2, fraction XI, of the Civil Registry law defines gender identity as a personal and internal conviction. The 2018 reform also amended article 133 of the Ley para la Familia de Coahuila de Zaragoza, so the change reached the state's family law alongside the registry.

Use of the procedure is documented. The director of Coahuila's Civil Registry, Ricardo Malacara, said that between early 2019 and March 2023 around 1,500 people in the state completed the legal gender-identity change before the registry, in both directions, male to female and female to male.
tangentialFactors: The 2018 reform was not a single-party measure. El Heraldo de Saltillo reported on 13 November 2018 that the Ley del Registro Civil del Estado presented to the plenary drew on proposals from several parliamentary groups together with an initiative by former governor Ruben Moreira, and that the dictamen was approved unanimously. The paper described the measure as proposing legal recognition of trans people under their new legal personality.
localsOnly: Employment figures for trans residents of Coahuila were reported by the state's Civil Registry director in March 2023: approximately 3,500 transgender citizens held formal jobs at companies operating in the state.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Coahuila-specific information was identified on how the state's criminal code treats hate motivation, on prosecutions or convictions for violence against trans people in the state, or on how registry offices apply the recognition procedure in practice. Sources reviewed do not establish whether the state procedure is open to trans people who are not resident in Coahuila, nor how state registry records interact with federal identity documents.

The figure of roughly 1,500 completed procedures between early 2019 and March 2023 is a raw count; the source gives no population denominator for Coahuila, so it cannot be read as a rate of uptake or compared across states.
